newsitem.title: JAPAN: YEAREND - Japan mired in past as it confronts future.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Japan mired in past as it confronts future.

text.p: In the ancient Asian calendar, it was the Year of the Rat.

But the Roman god Janus -- a deity depicted with two heads facing in opposite directions -- might well have been a better symbol for a period which saw Japan mired in old-style scandals while struggling to craft a blueprint for its future.

After months spent licking wounds from the previous year's disasters, leaders started looking ahead and prescribed a raft of reforms for an economic system once seen as the source of Japan's post-war growth miracle but now viewed as an obstacle to future success.

Even as the promises were made, however, a tangle of scandals revealed the legacy of corruption bred by decades of often too-cosy ties within Japan's "Iron Triangle" of bureaucrats, business and politics.
A YEAR OF RELATIVE CALM

In contrast to 1995, when a massive earthquake in western Japan and a nerve gas attack on Tokyo's commuter-packed subways were followed by banking failures, a soaring yen and a stock market plunge, 1996 was a year of relative calm.

The dollar, having slumped last year to a record low of 79.75 yen, rose gradually from around 105 yen in January to close to 115 yen in October -- prompting Japanese authorities to suggest that the rise had gone far enough.
Keen to see Japan's modest economic recovery stay on track, the central bank kept interest rates at the rockbottom levels after slashing the official discount rate to 0.5 percent.
Japan's economy has been struggling to shake off the legacy of the 1980s investment "bubble" whose collapse left many companies burdened with bad loans and virtually valueless collateral.

U.S.-Japan ties, jolted in 1995 by nasty trade feuds and public antipathy to the huge American military presence on Japan's southern island of Okinawa, were mostly mended by an April leaders' summit in Tokyo.

Domestic political initiatives, meanwhile, were paralysed for much of the year, with the conservative Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) trapped in an uneasy partnership with once-rival Socialists and a tiny band of would-be reformers.
POLITICAL EQUATION ALTERED BY ELECTION

That political equation was altered by an October election which failed by a slim margin to give the LDP a majority but set the stage for the party's first return to sole power after being booted out by disgruntled voters in 1993.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto was quick off the mark at the start of his second term to promote an image as a bold reformer, unveiling sweeping -- although familiar -- proposals to open up Japan's lagging financial markets by the year 2001.
The reforms aim to reverse the decline of Japan's financial markets and put Tokyo back in the running with London and New York as a global centre.
Hashimoto also pledged to streamline central government ministries and promised to get the nation's bloated budget deficit under control.

A plethora of advisory panels, meanwhile, called for drastic cuts in the red tape and regulations that critics say smother competition in key sectors like telecommunications and prevent Japan's promise of higher growth from being fulfilled.
DOUBTS OVER REFORM PERSIST, UNDERLINED BY SCANDALS
Doubts, however, persist over how committed the LDP is to reform and how keen business leaders really are to see their frequent and loud calls for change implemented.
"Expectations (about reform) have been raised, so in that sense Japan is looking into the future," said Jeff Young, an economist at Salomon Brothers Asia.
"But the question is whether there is the political will and public demand," Young added.
As if to underline those doubts, scandals emerged with relentless regularity, tarnishing Japan Inc's image and raising questions about corporate management and bureaucratic ethics.

Among the scandals were the huge losses piled up by a veteran copper trader at giant Sumitomo Corp and revelations that Health and Welfare Ministry officials in the 1980s sanctioned use of untreated blood products which led some 1,800 haemophiliacs to contract HIV, the virus that causes AIDS.

More recently, a new money-for-favours scandal surfaced at the Health and Welfare Ministry, while questions are also being raised about improper links among Trade Ministry bureaucrats and an oil wholesaler arrested for tax evasion.

The latter scandal blotted Tokyo's international copybook by keeping its trade minister from attending the recent ministerial conference in Singapore of the World Trade Organisation, a body whose praises Japan has sung loudly and often.
Despite the doubts about reform prospects, some businessmen and analysts believe it may well be the conservative old-guard that succeeds where self-styled anti-LDP reformers failed.

"Yes, the legacy of old-style money politics is strong within the LDP... but rather than just getting entrapped in the past, Hashimoto is trying to move ahead," said Jesper Koll, chief economist at JP Morgan in Tokyo recently.
"Japan is very good at a revolution from within."
